title: Mediastinal Masses and Widening
evidence_text: Mediastinal widening on chest radiograph is defined by a mediastinal width exceeding 8 cm on supine AP or 6 cm on erect PA projection. Differential diagnoses include mediastinal hematoma, lymphadenopathy, vascular aneurysm, thymoma, or projection magnification.
visual_concept: Mediastinal widening exceeding standard diagnostic thresholds (>8cm AP or >6cm PA).

title: Cardiomegaly Imaging and Evaluation
evidence_text: Cardiomegaly is recognized on posteroanterior (PA) chest radiographs when the cardiothoracic ratio (maximum transverse cardiac diameter divided by internal thoracic diameter) exceeds 0.50. On AP supine films, projection magnification may falsely elevate CTR up to 0.60.
visual_concept: Cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) exceeding 0.50 on PA projection.

title: Challenging Chest Radiograph Interpretation
evidence_text: Airspace opacities on chest radiographs may be associated with several processes, including pneumonia, aspiration, atelectasis, alveolar pulmonary edema, and pulmonary hemorrhage.
visual_concept: Increased pulmonary attenuation obscuring underlying bronchovascular markings.

title: Solitary Pulmonary Nodule and Pulmonary Mass
evidence_text: A pulmonary nodule is defined as a discrete, well-circumscribed radiographic opacity less than or equal to 3 cm in diameter surrounded by aerated lung parenchyma without associated adenopathy, atelectasis, or pleural effusion. Lesions larger than 3 cm are defined as pulmonary masses.
visual_concept: Discrete solitary or multiple circumscribed nodule (<3cm) or mass (>3cm).

title: Pulmonary Edema Radiographic Findings
evidence_text: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema typically progresses from pulmonary venous hypertension (upper lobe blood diversion) to interstitial edema (peribronchial cuffing, Kerley B lines, perihilar haze) and finally alveolar edema with classic bat-wing / butterfly alveolar infiltrates.
visual_concept: Peribronchial cuffing, Kerley B lines, and bat-wing perihilar consolidation.

title: Airspace Disease and Lung Consolidation
evidence_text: Consolidation refers to the replacement of alveolar gas by cellular exudate, transudate, blood, or neoplastic tissue. Cardinal radiographic signs include homogeneous dense airspace opacity, preservation of lung volume, air bronchograms, and the silhouette sign.
visual_concept: Homogeneous dense airspace filling with visible air bronchograms and silhouette sign.

title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia Imaging
evidence_text: Chest radiography is the reference diagnostic imaging standard for suspected pneumonia, demonstrating focal or multifocal parenchymal consolidation, patchy alveolar infiltrates, or interstitial opacities correlating with respiratory infection symptoms.
visual_concept: Patchy or confluent focal alveolar infiltrate with ill-defined margins.

title: Atelectasis: Radiographic Features and Mechanisms
evidence_text: Atelectasis represents the collapse or incomplete expansion of pulmonary parenchyma. Direct radiographic signs include displacement of interlobar fissures and crowded vascular markings; indirect signs include diaphragmatic elevation, mediastinal shift toward the collapsed lobe, and compensatory hyperinflation.
visual_concept: Linear horizontal plate-like opacity or triangular wedge of volume loss.

title: Pneumothorax: Imaging and Evaluation
evidence_text: Pneumothorax is identified on erect chest radiographs by a thin, sharp white line representing the visceral pleura separated from the chest wall by a peripheral radiolucent space devoid of bronchovascular markings.
visual_concept: Sharp visceral pleural white line with peripheral radiolucent space devoid of markings.

title: Pleural Effusion Imaging
evidence_text: Free-flowing pleural effusion collects in dependent pleural recesses, producing blunting of the posterior costophrenic angle on lateral films (>50 mL) and lateral costophrenic angle blunting on erect frontal radiographs (>175 mL), accompanied by a characteristic fluid meniscus sign.
visual_concept: Blunting of lateral/posterior costophrenic angle with fluid meniscus sign.

title: Pleural Disease and Calcification
evidence_text: Non-effusion pleural abnormalities on chest radiography include diffuse or focal pleural thickening, fibrothorax, and calcified pleural plaques (often along the diaphragmatic or posterolateral parietal pleura), characteristic of prior hemothorax, empyema, or mineral exposure.
visual_concept: Focal pleural thickening, nodularity, or calcified plaques along parietal pleura.

title: Rib and Thoracic Skeletal Fractures
evidence_text: Thoracic cage fractures are identified on chest radiographs by cortical disruption, cortical step deformity, offset of bony trabeculae, or displacement of bone fragments along the ribs, clavicles, scapulae, or thoracic vertebrae.
visual_concept: Disruption of cortical bone margin, lucent fracture line, or step deformity.

title: Radiographic Evaluation of Thoracic Lines and Tubes
evidence_text: Chest radiography is essential for verifying proper anatomical positioning of invasive thoracic hardware, including endotracheal tubes (tip 3-5 cm above the carina), central venous catheters (tip at the cavoatrial junction), nasogastric tubes (tip subdiaphragmatic in stomach), chest tubes, and cardiac pacemakers.
visual_concept: Radio-opaque tubing, catheters, pacing leads, or monitoring electrodes.

title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Emphysema
evidence_text: Classic radiographic signs of pulmonary emphysema include lung hyperinflation, flattened diaphragmatic domes (visualized on both frontal and lateral views), increased retrosternal airspace (>2.5 cm), attenuated peripheral vasculature ('vascular deficiency'), and occasional bullae.
visual_concept: Bilateral lung hyperlucency, low flattened diaphragms, and attenuated vascular caliber.

title: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis Imaging Evaluation
evidence_text: Radiographic manifestations of pulmonary fibrosis feature bilateral basilar-predominant reticular opacities, traction bronchiectasis, peripheral honeycombing, and progressive loss of lung volume with architectural distortion.
visual_concept: Basilar reticular markings, volume loss, and subpleural honeycombing.

title: Solitary Pulmonary Nodule Imaging Guidelines
evidence_text: A solitary pulmonary nodule is defined as an intraparenchymal rounded or oval opacity measuring up to 30 mm in diameter, surrounded by aerated lung without associated atelectasis, adenopathy, or pleural effusion.
visual_concept: Circumscribed spherical opacity measuring <=30 mm.

title: Evaluation of Pulmonary Masses on Chest Radiography
evidence_text: A pulmonary mass is defined as any focal thoracic opacity measuring strictly greater than 30 mm in diameter. Given the high probability of malignancy, urgent diagnostic cross-sectional CT and biopsy evaluation are warranted.
visual_concept: Focal soft-tissue density opacity measuring strictly >30 mm.

title: Pleural Disease and Fibrothorax
evidence_text: Diffuse pleural thickening appears as a continuous, smooth or nodular layer of soft tissue along the lateral thoracic wall exceeding 3 mm in thickness, often extending across multiple intercostal spaces and blunting costophrenic angles.
visual_concept: Continuous soft-tissue pleural mantle along the rib cage.

title: Thoracic Calcifications: Benign versus Pathologic Patterns
evidence_text: Pulmonary calcifications appear as dense, radio-opaque mineralized deposits. Concentric, central, or popcorn calcifications in nodules indicate benign granulomatous or hamartomatous etiology, whereas eccentric or punctate calcifications may indicate neoplasm.
visual_concept: High-attenuation dense mineralized radio-opaque deposits.

title: Hiatal and Diaphragmatic Hernias on Chest Radiography
evidence_text: Diaphragmatic and hiatal hernias present on chest radiography as retrocardiac masses containing gas bubbles or an air-fluid level, representing intrathoracic displacement of the stomach or bowel through the esophageal hiatus or congenital defects.
visual_concept: Retrocardiac air-fluid level or mass projecting above the diaphragm.

title: Pneumoperitoneum Detection on Erect Chest Radiography
evidence_text: Erect frontal chest radiography is the most sensitive plain film for detecting free intra-abdominal air (subdiaphragmatic crescentic lucency), identifying as little as 1-2 mL of free gas under the right hemidiaphragm dome. Highly indicative of visceral perforation.
visual_concept: Free crescentic gas under the right or left hemidiaphragm.

title: Scoliosis Evaluation and Thoracic Cavity Deformity
evidence_text: Scoliosis is defined as a lateral spinal curvature with a Cobb angle exceeding 10 degrees on upright radiograph. Severe thoracic curvature causes asymmetry of the hemithoraces, rib crowding, and rotational displacement of the mediastinum.
visual_concept: Lateral spinal curvature exceeding 10 degrees with rib rotational deformity.

title: Radiological Patterns of Pulmonary Tuberculosis
evidence_text: Reactivation pulmonary tuberculosis predominantly involves apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes, showing patchy consolidation, thick-walled cavitations, endobronchial spread (tree-in-bud nodularity), and apical pleural scarring.
visual_concept: Apical fibro-cavitary consolidation and endobronchial nodularity.

title: Radiologic Diagnosis of Bronchiectasis
evidence_text: Chest radiograph signs of bronchiectasis include parallel linear densities ('tram-track lines' representing thickened bronchial walls), ring shadows with or without air-fluid levels (dilated cystic bronchi), and localized atelectasis.
visual_concept: Tram-track parallel bronchial lines and cystic ring shadows.

title: Subcutaneous Thoracic Emphysema Clinical Presentation
evidence_text: Subcutaneous emphysema appears on chest radiographs as striated, comb-like lucencies outlining muscle bundles along the lateral chest wall, pectoralis major muscle ('gingko leaf sign'), and neck soft tissues.
visual_concept: Comb-like gas lucencies outlining muscle bundles and soft tissues.

title: Rib Fractures and Thoracic Trauma
evidence_text: Acute rib fractures present as sharp cortical disruptions, radiolucent fracture lines, or offset fragment step-offs along the posterior, lateral, or anterior rib arcs, frequently accompanied by localized pleural thickening or pneumothorax.
visual_concept: Sharp cortical step-off or radiolucent line crossing rib cortex.

title: Tracheobronchial Foreign Body Aspiration and Ingestion
evidence_text: Radio-opaque foreign bodies (coins, hardware, pins, dental prostheses) are directly visible on chest radiographs. Radiolucent foreign bodies are inferred by indirect secondary signs: obstructive atelectasis, focal air-trapping, or mediastinal shift.
visual_concept: Radio-opaque exogenous object or localized unilateral hyperinflation.

title: Normal Chest Radiograph Interpretation Standards
evidence_text: A standard normal frontal chest radiograph demonstrates well-aerated bilateral lung fields without focal consolidation or mass, normal cardiothoracic ratio (<0.50), sharp costophrenic angles, normal mediastinal width, and intact skeletal cage contours.
visual_concept: Clear bilateral parenchyma, sharp angles, normal cardiothoracic ratio.
